opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it really came out of the economics of how we were scaling at the time. Query traffic was growing really quickly, and the way we handled more traffic was to add more replicas of the index. Each replica was sharded across a bunch of machines, and the index itself lived on disk, so every query meant a lot of disk seeks across all those shards. Disks are slow for random access, so latency and throughput were basically bound by how many seeks you could do.

At some point we looked at it and realized that with the number of machines we had in each replica, if you added up all the memory across them, it was actually enough to hold a full copy of the index in memory. Once you see that, the question flips. Instead of "how do we squeeze more out of these disks," it's "why are we touching disk at all?"

Moving to an in-memory index gave us a big jump in throughput per machine and much lower latency. It also changed what we could afford to do per query. Lots of things that were too expensive with disk seeks suddenly became cheap. We could look at more candidate documents, do more expensive scoring, and add things like query expansion with synonyms, because the cost of a lookup dropped dramatically.

It wasn't entirely free. You have to think much harder about failures, about how you lay out the data so it's compact, and about how you roll out new index versions without disrupting serving. But the core insight was simple. Hardware ratios had shifted, and if you redo the back-of-the-envelope math when that happens, sometimes the right architecture is completely different from what you've been doing. That kind of thinking, knowing your latency numbers and asking what the system would look like if you designed it today, has stayed with me ever since.

r001.rationale: The response discusses disk seeks and latency, but does not say that increasing the number of shards as the index grows keeps query latency bounded.

r002.rationale: It says query traffic was growing and that they handled more traffic by adding replicas of the index, with each replica distributed across shards.

r003.rationale: It says the machines in each serving replica had enough aggregate memory to hold a full copy of the index, and presents that realization as the reason to move away from disk.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it wasn't really one grand decision so much as a response to pain we were feeling at the time. Around 2000, 2001, the index was growing fast, query traffic was growing fast, and the way we served queries was pretty conventional: the index was sharded across machines, each shard lived on disk, and a query would go to all the shards and each one would do a bunch of disk seeks to pull in the posting lists for the query terms. And disk seeks are just brutally slow relative to everything else. You're talking about milliseconds per seek on hardware that could do a lot of computation in a millisecond. So latency was dominated by waiting on disks, and throughput was capped by how many seeks per second a machine could do.

The thing that made the in-memory approach plausible was looking at the actual numbers rather than the conventional wisdom. Conventional wisdom said indexes are too big for memory, you keep them on disk. But if you did the arithmetic on the size of the compressed index, the cost per gigabyte of RAM at the time, and the number of machines we were already buying anyway because we needed the disk spindles and CPUs, it turned out that spreading the index across enough commodity machines and holding each shard in memory wasn't that much more expensive than what we were doing. And the win was enormous: an order of magnitude or more improvement in query throughput per machine, much lower and much more predictable latency, and it opened up a lot of flexibility in how we could do ranking, because you could afford to look at more data per query when touching it was essentially free.

There was some risk. Memory was more expensive than disk, and you have the problem that if a machine dies you've lost that shard until you reload it, so you need replication and good failover. But we already had to deal with machines failing all the time because we were using pretty cheap hardware, so a lot of the fault tolerance machinery was already something we were building. Sanjay Ghemawat and I spent a lot of time on the serving system and the compression formats so that the index would actually fit, and so that the index-building side could produce shards that were efficiently laid out for memory access rather than disk access.

I think the broader lesson I took from it, and which came up again and again later, is that it pays to periodically redo the back-of-the-envelope calculation. Hardware ratios change, and a design that was clearly right three years earlier can become clearly wrong, and often nobody notices because the system still works. If you know roughly how long a memory reference takes versus a disk seek versus a network round trip, you can sketch out two or three alternative designs in an afternoon and see which one is actually bounded by the right resource. That's more or less what happened here.

r001.rationale: It describes a growing index and sharding, but does not say that increasing the shard count keeps query latency bounded.

r002.rationale: It mentions replication for fault tolerance and failover, but does not say that adding replicas increases capacity to serve growing query traffic.

r003.rationale: It says the compressed index could be spread across the commodity machines Google already needed, with each shard held in memory, making the full index’s in-memory placement feasible.

astra-6.text:
Well, the basic motivation was latency. When you’re answering a search query, you need to look up information in the index, and disk seeks are quite expensive compared with memory accesses. So we started looking at whether we could keep the index in the aggregate memory of a collection of machines.

The important thing is that it didn’t have to fit on one machine. We were already distributing the index across many machines, so the question was: how much memory would each machine need, and what would that cost? And then, what would we gain in query throughput as well as latency?

If you just compare the cost of a byte of RAM with a byte of disk, RAM looks expensive. But if keeping the index in memory lets each machine serve substantially more queries, the economics look different. That was the key: looking at the cost of serving searches, rather than just the cost of storing the index.

r001.rationale: It discusses memory’s latency benefit and distributing the index, but does not explain that adding shards as the index grows keeps query latency bounded.

r002.rationale: It mentions query throughput, but does not explain that adding replicas of each shard increases capacity for growing query traffic.

r003.rationale: It considers fitting the index in the aggregate memory of a machine collection, but does not state that a complete index could fit in the machines already needed to serve traffic or identify that realization as the basis for the 2001 move.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the key observation was that memory was getting cheaper, and you didn’t need the whole index to fit in one machine. You could partition it across a lot of machines, with each one holding a piece.

With a disk-based index, you spend a lot of time waiting for seeks. Keeping the index in memory meant we could examine more of it in the same amount of time, which was useful both for latency and for search quality. You could consider more candidates and do more work to find good results.

Of course, you had to look at the economics of the whole system. Memory was more expensive than disk per byte, but if each machine could serve more queries, that could make the overall system more attractive. So it was really a combination of the hardware trends and thinking about the cost per query, rather than just the cost of storing the index.

r001.rationale: The response mentions partitioning the index and latency, but does not explain that increasing shard count as the index grows keeps query latency bounded.

r002.rationale: It says each machine could serve more queries, but does not explain adding replicas of each shard to handle growing query traffic.

r003.rationale: It describes distributing the index across machines, but does not identify that the full index could fit in the aggregate memory of machines already needed to serve traffic.
